new_entities.name: Testosterone replacement in hypogonadal men
new_entities.description: Exogenous testosterone therapy given to symptomatic men with documented low testosterone.

edges.effect_quant: In the Testosterone Trials bone substudy, testosterone increased spine trabecular volumetric bone density by 7.5% versus 0.8% with placebo over one year, for a treatment effect of 6.8% (95% CI 4.8% to 8.7%).
edges.population: older or middle-aged hypogonadal men with low testosterone, including men at risk of frailty or bone loss
edges.mechanism: This is classic hormone replacement physiology: restoring testosterone improves bone remodeling partly through direct androgen effects and partly through aromatization to estradiol. The bone-density signal is more convincing than many lifestyle-facing testosterone claims because it is supported by objective imaging outcomes rather than subjective symptom scales alone.
edges.summary: Testosterone replacement improves bone mineral density in hypogonadal men, especially at the spine and in trabecular-rich compartments. The evidence is stronger for density and estimated strength than for actual fracture prevention, but the bone response itself is one of the more solid benefits of treatment.
edges.caveats: Higher bone density does not automatically prove lower long-term fracture risk, particularly over short follow-up. The benefit also needs to be weighed against other treatment risks and should not be confused with a general anti-aging indication in men without documented hypogonadism.

evidence.citation: Snyder PJ et al 2017 JAMA Intern Med
evidence.notes: Effect of Testosterone Treatment on Volumetric Bone Density and Strength in Older Men With Low Testosterone: A Controlled Clinical Trial.

effect_quant.comparator: testosterone versus placebo for change in spine trabecular volumetric bone mineral density

evidence.citation: Grossmann M et al 2021 J Clin Endocrinol Metab
